events.text: Day 1 begins.

No one has given us anything concrete yet, so I’m not going to invent a suspicion on Day 1. I’ll be watching how people frame their reads and, more importantly, how the vote lines up later. For now, I’d rather hear substance than forced accusations.

I agree with Leo's approach — it's still early and we don't have much to work with yet. That said, I think Day 1 is important for establishing how people present themselves. I want to see who's willing to make firm reads and who plays it safe from the start. A couple of people commenting on tone rather than content tends to stand out to me. I'll keep watching for that as the day develops.

Omar, you say people commenting on tone rather than content stand out, but so far we have very little content to evaluate. What specifically would you consider suspicious about that, rather than just normal early-day uncertainty?

Fair point, Amara. To clarify — I'm not saying commenting on tone is inherently suspicious on its own. What I meant is that as the day develops, I'll be watching whether people keep making surface-level observations about how others come across without ever committing to a real read. Early on, everyone does it; the pattern becomes telling if someone never moves past it. I don't currently find your question itself suspicious — it's a reasonable push for specifics, and I'd rather people challenge vague statements than let them slide. What does concern me slightly is Leo's opening post, which essentially says 'I'll wait and see' while also framing that as a virtue. It's a comfortable position because it costs nothing to take. I'm not accusing Leo of anything yet, but I'd like to see what Felix, Zara, and the rest of the quiet players have to say before anyone locks in firm reads. The more people stay silent on Day 1, the harder it becomes to distinguish coasting from genuine observation.

Omar, fair hit. My opening was cautious, and I can see why it reads as cost-free. I don’t want to hide behind “wait and see.” At this point my only mild concern is that you’ve spent more energy framing how others should play than committing to a read yourself, though your push on Amara was reasonable. Amara’s question also felt like normal early pressure. I’d like to hear from Zara, Felix, and the quieter players, but I’m not going to pretend silence alone is damning. Omar, you mentioned wanting to see what Felix and Zara say before locking reads — do you have any actual lean on either of them now, or is it still just a watch list?

Leo, to answer your question directly — no, I don't have a real lean on Felix or Zara yet. I named them because they've been silent and I want to see where they land, but silence on Day 1 isn't enough for me to call anyone scummy. I'd rather hear them speak than pre-judge them for staying quiet. My current soft read, if I'm being honest, is still the one I already flagged: your opening post. Not because it was wrong — it was reasonable — but because it was the kind of statement that plays well from any alignment. Saying 'I'll wait for substance' costs a mafia player nothing, and it scores points for appearing measured. What would actually help me is if you told me who you're *most* watching right now, even if it's soft. I gave you my concern; I'd like to see if you have one for anyone else or if you're still entirely on the sidelines. If your answer is 'nobody stands out yet,' that's fine — but I want it on the record so we can compare against how your reads develop later.

Omar, direct answer: my current soft watch is you. Not simply because you pushed me — that was fair enough — but because you’ve asked me to commit while your own read has stayed at “Leo’s opening was cautious and cost-free.” That may be a real concern, but it’s also a safe one to keep repeating without much movement. I’m not calling you mafia for it yet. I’m saying I want your read to develop past style if you expect mine to. Amara’s question to you felt like normal early pressure, and I don’t think silence from Zara or Felix is damning by itself. My position is: I’ll judge people by whether their reads sharpen once there’s actual back-and-forth, not by who was quiet first. For now, Omar is the player I’m watching most.

I’m Sam. I’ve read the Omar/Leo exchange. My take: Omar’s push on Leo’s opening wasn’t unfair, but Leo has a point that Omar’s own read hasn’t moved much past style. On Day 1 I don’t want to treat caution as scumminess; plenty of town players open carefully. What matters is whether reads sharpen after pressure. I’m null on both for now. Amara, your question to Omar was a good specificity check: after Omar clarified that he was watching for a pattern over time, did that answer satisfy you, or do you think he’s still leaning too much on how people frame things rather than substance? I’m asking because your read on that exchange will help me judge whether the pressure was genuine or just early noise. I’m not voting or accusing yet.

Sam, Omar’s clarification satisfied my original question: watching for a persistent pattern is different from treating early caution as suspicious by itself. His concern about Leo’s opening is fair but weak, since it could fit either alignment. Leo’s observation that Omar’s read has stayed narrow is fair too, though there hasn’t been much else to evaluate. I’m null on both for now.

Zara, how do you assess that exchange? Is either player’s response to pressure more concerning to you, and why?

Thanks for bringing me in, Amara. Looking at the back-and-forth between Omar and Leo, neither strikes me as clearly scummy, but Omar's side felt slightly more strained to me. Omar criticized Leo's opening for being safe and 'cost-free,' yet Omar's own initial remark about people commenting on tone was just as broad and non-committal. While Omar gave a reasonable defense to your question about tracking patterns over time, he then repeatedly demanded that Leo commit to reads while keeping his own ledger completely clear. Leo's pivot back onto Omar was somewhat reactive, but he did at least answer the questions asked of him plainly. To me, it reads like an early procedural dispute where both players focused heavily on tone and posture rather than genuine scum-hunting. If I had to pick, Omar's insistence on framing Leo's caution as suspect feels a touch more manufactured, though it's still early. I'm curious to see how others view it before drawing firm conclusions.

I've been reading the Omar/Leo exchange closely, and here's where I land. Both players have been reasonable so far, but I want to push back on one thing from each side. Omar, your core concern — that Leo's opening was a cost-free position — is legitimate on its face, but you've now restated it three times without escalating it into anything actionable. At some point, a repeated soft concern becomes its own form of the caution you're criticizing. If it's a real read, sharpen it; if it isn't, drop it. Leo, I'll say the opposite to you: naming Omar as your top watch was the right move, and I take it at face value, but your justification was mostly a mirror of his own critique. I'd like your watch on him to be grounded in something he's actually done, not just the symmetry of the argument, because symmetric reasoning is easy to produce regardless of alignment. On Amara and Sam: both of you asked clarifying questions rather than making reads, and both questions were genuinely useful — they forced specifics out of a vague exchange. I don't read anything into that yet. Zara, your lean toward Omar being slightly more manufactured is the first directional statement anyone has made, and I notice you buffered it heavily with 'it's still early' and 'before drawing firm conclusions.' That's fine on Day 1, but I'll be tracking whether that lean actually develops or stays parked at 'slightly, sort of.' For the still-quiet players — Priya, Elena, Felix — no pressure, but the exchange we've had so far is entirely about tone and posture between two people who both agreed the disagreement was mostly procedural. I'd rather spend my attention on what the next few statements add in substance than relitigate whether Omar or Leo was marginally more guarded. Right now I'm null on everyone. My only genuine note is a process one: the most informative thing so far hasn't been the accusations, it's been who volunteered directional reads when asked — Leo did, Zara did softly, Omar hasn't really beyond his Leo concern. That's a weak signal at best on Day 1, and I'm not weighting it heavily yet, but I'm noting it for later comparison.

Felix here, so I'm speaking up after a quiet opening. I've read the Omar/Leo exchange and I agree with Isha that it has mostly been about tone and posture. Omar's point that Leo's opening was cost-free is a fair observation, but it's still a soft read that hasn't moved much. Leo's pivot onto Omar was defensive, though he did answer Amara's and Sam's questions plainly. I'm null on everyone right now. I'm not going to invent a lean just to look active. Zara, you said Omar's framing felt slightly manufactured. Which specific line or move made it feel that way to you, rather than just the general tone?

Felix, to answer your question specifically: what stood out most was in Omar's message where he pushed Leo to name his top watch and put it 'on the record so we can compare against how your reads develop later.' Setting up a benchmark for someone else to be judged against later is a classic scum-hunting tool, but doing so right after dismissing any scrutiny on himself for not having reads—and while repeatedly noting that Leo's stance was 'cost-free'—felt unbalanced. Omar created liability for Leo while keeping his own ledger completely clear of any commitments. That specific push to lock Leo into a stance, rather than organically exploring thoughts together, felt a bit forced and procedural to me. Felix, looking back at that specific demand in Omar's post, do you see it as routine town pressure to generate discussion, or do you also see an asymmetry in how he applied expectations to Leo versus himself?

Zara, to answer you directly: I see some asymmetry in Omar's post, but I don't think it's a strong signal yet. Asking Leo to commit to a top watch is a normal way to generate discussion, and Leo did answer plainly. Where I agree with you is that Omar asked Leo for a benchmark to be judged against later while offering nothing of his own beyond the Leo concern. That's the part I'd weigh. I'm still null on everyone and not voting. Omar, you set the record-keeping standard, so I'd like your answer: what is your current watch, even if it's soft, and what would change it?

I appreciate Felix's perspective. It's completely reasonable to see Omar’s prompt as standard town prodding, but that asymmetry is precisely why it caught my attention. When a player constructs an exacting standard for someone else to be judged against while deliberately shielding themselves from offering any commitments of their own, that is often how scum maintain an appearance of rigor without incurring any personal risk.

Isha, to address your earlier note: you pointed out that my read on Omar was heavily buffered with qualifiers and said you'd be tracking whether it actually develops or stays parked. To be direct about where I stand: I'm not going to rush a vote on Omar when Priya and Elena have yet to speak, but between Leo and Omar, Omar's framing remains the more calculated and self-preserving of the two to me. Given that Felix also acknowledged that specific asymmetry in Omar demanding a baseline from Leo without providing one of his own, where do you currently land on that point? Do you still view the back-and-forth as purely procedural noise, or does that pattern give you any tangible directional read?

Zara, since you yielded to me, I'll answer your question directly: I still view the Omar/Leo exchange as mostly procedural noise, but with one directional note attached. The asymmetry you and Felix both identified is real — Omar set up a benchmark for Leo to be judged against while his own ledger stayed clear of any commitment beyond the Leo concern itself. I weight it lightly, though, because it's a single exchange, and town players demand commitments from others while hesitating on their own reads all the time on Day 1. It's not a pattern yet; it's one data point.

What I'm actually tracking is the process observation I made earlier. When pressure was applied, Leo committed — he named Omar as his top watch and gave a reason. You committed, softly but directionally. Felix explicitly stated null and explained his standard. Omar, across three turns, has produced style critiques and requests for others to commit, but no directional output of his own beyond restating the Leo concern. That's a weak signal on its own, and I said I wouldn't weight it heavily — but it's the same shape as the asymmetry you're describing, just viewed from the commitment side instead of the benchmark side.

So where do I land? Soft lean toward watching Omar, nowhere near a vote. The clean test is Felix's question, which Omar hasn't answered yet: what is your current watch, and what would change it? If Omar answers with substance — even a soft directional read with a reason — that largely clears my note. If he deflects again into meta-commentary about how reads should form and what other people ought to do, that strengthens it considerably. I want that answer on the record before anyone forms stronger opinions either way.

Felix, I'll say your framing was the most useful in this exchange: you identified the asymmetry accurately but refused to overweight it, and you separated 'normal town prodding' from 'the part I'd weigh.' That's the standard I'd like the rest of the thread to hold itself to — pressure with precision, not pressure for its own sake.

One last thing before I finish: Priya and Elena have not spoken at all yet. I'm not going to treat silence as damning, and I said that earlier — but two players being entirely absent from the only substantive exchange we've had means their first reads will carry extra information, simply because they're arriving with no entanglement in the Omar/Leo dispute. I'd genuinely like to hear how they assess it with fresh eyes.

First words from me, so let me be precise about what I bring and what I don't. I wasn't in the Omar/Leo exchange, I have no stake in it, and I've had no chance to form an opinion about anyone's alignment from tone alone — so I'm not going to pretend I have one.

What I can say is this. Zara and Felix independently converged on the same specific feature: Omar asked Leo to name a top watch and put it on the record for later comparison, while offering nothing of his own beyond a restatement of that opening-post concern. Isha framed the same shape from the other side — who committed under pressure and who didn't. Three players describing one exchange and landing on the same structural observation is mildly more interesting than one player noticing it, but it's still one exchange between two people who agreed at multiple points that their disagreement was mostly procedural. I weight it lightly. Town players absolutely do press others for reads while hedging their own — usually because a firm early read is worth more than a fast one, and being wrong in public on Day 1 is expensive. That logic cuts toward town just as easily as toward mafia.

What I do want to flag is a small procedural thing about our discussion rather than about any player. We have spent six substantive turns on a two-person stylistic dispute that both participants characterize as minor, while Sam, Amara, Felix and Zara have all said they're null, and Isha has said he's null with a soft watch. Felix asked Omar a clean, answerable question — what is your current watch, even soft, and what would change it — and that question is still open. An open question sitting unanswered is more informative than another round of paraphrase. If Omar answers with substance, the note largely clears. If he deflects into meta-commentary about how reads should form, that's the second data point and it would matter more than anything said so far.

So my own position: I'm null on nearly everyone, including Omar. I won't be voting on a style critique alone.

Elena, you're the one person besides me who hasn't had a turn at all, and you've been outside this entire dispute — which means your first impression is the least contaminated read in the thread. I genuinely want to know it, and I want to know it before I settle anything: how do you read the exchange between Omar and Leo, and what, if anything, about the way this discussion has run stands out to you as worth pushing on? I'd rather hear your unanchored take than the room's consensus.

Thanks, Priya. Stepping in with fresh eyes, my biggest takeaway isn’t actually about Omar or Leo—it’s about the state of the thread itself. The first thing everyone needs to realize is mechanical: Omar, Leo, and Zara have all used all three of their Day 1 speaking turns. When Felix, Isha, and Priya all framed their next step around waiting to see how Omar answers Felix’s question, we are waiting on something that literally cannot happen. Omar has no turns left to respond, clarify, or commit today.

Because of that, continuing to treat Omar’s silence from here on out as evasion or deflection would be a mistake. As for the exchange itself when it happened: I saw it as a classic Day 1 procedural skirmish. Omar tried to apply pressure on Leo’s safe opening, and while his demand for Leo to establish a benchmark was asymmetric compared to his own caution, it’s a standard early town poke just as easily as it is calculated scum maneuvering. Leo’s defensive mirror was equally standard. What struck me as slightly more opportunistic was how Zara seized on that asymmetry and burned through all three of her turns prosecuting Omar for it, keeping the spotlight locked onto an early spat rather than widening the field. But since Zara is also out of turns, litigating that further right now won't produce new information.

We need to look at the players who still have turns and haven’t committed to much. Specifically, Sam entered at e9, made a safe null remark, asked Amara a clarifying question, and hasn't spoken since while half the room burned through their allotments.

Sam, since you have two turns remaining and the Omar/Leo thread is mechanically closed: looking beyond those two, who on this board has drawn your attention, and what do you make of the way the conversation stalled around them?

Elena, direct answer: beyond Omar/Leo, what drew my attention is how quickly the room treated Felix’s open question as the thread’s decisive test, even though Omar had no turns left to answer it. I include myself in that—my e9 was a safe null and a clarifying question, and I haven’t done enough to sharpen since. I’m not going to scumread Omar for silence that is mechanically forced. My soft concern right now is Zara: she made the first directional read on Omar, then spent her remaining turns restating the same asymmetry. That could be legitimate pressure, but it also kept the spotlight on one early spat while other players stayed vague. I don’t think it’s damning, and she’s out of turns, so I’m not voting on it. I’m null on most of the board and want to judge people by what they do with remaining turns, not by who was quiet first.

Amara, you asked the early specificity question and then stayed null on the Omar/Leo exchange. After Elena’s mechanical point, do you still see that exchange as mostly noise, and do you think Zara’s repeated focus on Omar was legitimate pressure or opportunistic tunneling? I’m asking because your answer will help me decide whether my soft concern has substance or is just style.

Sam, I still see the Omar/Leo exchange as weak evidence. Elena is right: Omar had already used all three turns when Felix asked him to clarify, so his lack of an answer tells us nothing.

Zara’s focus could be genuine pressure, but I’m mildly concerned that she described Omar as deliberately shielding himself from commitments. He had already named Leo as his soft concern, even if he repeated it rather than developing it. That makes her characterization stronger than the evidence warrants. It’s a soft watch, not a vote: Zara also answered Felix’s request for a specific example, which was useful.

Amara, your e21 tracks with me: Zara’s language was stronger than the evidence, and since Omar had no turns left, treating his non-answer as evasion would be unfair. My soft concern remains Zara for overcommitting to one early procedural read while the board stayed vague, but it is not a vote and she cannot respond today. Elena’s e19 was useful mechanically, but it also redirected attention from the Omar/Leo thread onto me and Zara right after that thread became closed; I want to know whether that was genuine fresh-eyes sorting or a convenient pivot. Priya, you were the player who most clearly framed Elena as the least contaminated read before she spoke. Now that Elena has spoken and immediately shifted the focus to me and Zara, how do you read that shift specifically in e19—does it look like legitimate process work from outside the dispute, or does it feel like choosing a safe target once the earlier exchange was mechanically closed? I’m asking about that specific pivot, not for a general read on Elena.

Sam, direct answer to your question about e19, since you asked me specifically. Elena's pivot was mixed, and I'll separate the two halves. The legitimate half: at e19 the players who could still generate new information were Sam, Isha, Felix, Elena and me — Omar, Leo and Zara were mechanically finished. So redirecting toward players with turns remaining was correct process work, and calling out the closed Omar thread was the single most useful thing said today. The convenient half: having identified that the field of still-active players was five, Elena then narrowed attention to exactly two of them — Sam and Zara — with Zara being out of turns and therefore unable to respond, and she never revisited Isha, Felix or me, who were also live. Pointing the room at others while spending none of her own remaining turns on substance is the asymmetry I care about, not the pivot itself. To be fair to her, she did invite fresh reads and explicitly said silence isn't damning. But she built the framing and then let it stand.

My position, stated plainly: null on most of the board. My soft concern is Zara, whose three turns went almost entirely to prosecuting Omar on a single exchange — but she cannot answer and I've already said I won't vote on a read I can't hear defended. So the live question is Elena. I'm not calling her mafia; I'm noting that her pivot was well-timed and that she has not spent a single one of her remaining turns since.

Elena, since you're the one I'm asking to answer, please address e19 specifically: after naming five players with turns remaining, why did you focus on Sam and Zara and leave Isha, Felix and me out of the new line of inquiry? And do you want to claim a role — police or doctor — or stay unclaimed? Everyone with turns left, please state your claim tonight; on a board this quiet, claims are worth more than tone.

Priya, to answer your first question directly: I did not focus on Sam and Zara as dual targets. I explicitly pointed out that Zara was out of turns and that continuing to litigate her would yield no new information; I only mentioned her to contextualize how the room had been trapped in that procedural loop. Among the players with turns left at that moment, Isha and Felix had just provided detailed breakdowns (e12, e13, e15, e17), and you had literally just passed the floor to me. Sam was the only person who had made a single safe post (e9) and remained silent since. Calling on Sam was the most direct way to get an uncommitted, live player to speak.

Now to your second question: absolutely not, and nobody else should claim either. Calling for power roles—police or doctor—to claim on Day 1 when there is no guilty report and no player facing an unavoidable miselimination is fundamentally damaging to town. In a nine-player setup with two mafia, outing our protective and investigative roles right now gives mafia all the information they need to dismantle town's night actions with zero guesswork. I am a plain villager, but under no circumstances should real power roles out themselves.

Only four of us—you, me, Isha, and Felix—even have turns remaining. A mass claim from this tiny subset virtually hands mafia the cop and doctor on a silver platter. Priya, why are you actively fishing for power role claims on Day 1 on an unpressured board? What town utility did you think outing the doctor or police would accomplish right now?

Elena, direct answer on the claims question: you're right, and I withdraw it. Asking the live players to state police/doctor claims on an unpressured Day 1 board was a bad call on my part — I was trying to manufacture information, and the utility argument I gave doesn't survive contact with the actual setup. With two mafia still hidden, a mass claim hands them exactly the targets they need. I'm not claiming any role tonight, and I don't think anyone should. What I should have said was "claim only if you have a reason to," not a blanket demand for everyone with turns left.

On alignment, here's my honest state. My soft lean is Omar, and I'll own that it's soft, and that he cannot answer it today. The reason is not silence. Elena correctly closed that thread: Omar was out of turns before Felix asked, so his non-answer carries no weight. The reason is the shape across all three of his turns — he demanded a benchmark from Leo, restated the same cost-free critique three times without escalating it, and never produced a directional read of his own. Isha and Zara independently found that same shape, though from opposite angles.

But I want to flag the counterweight honestly: Leo and Zara both converged on Omar, and that convergence has two explanations — two honest readers found the same weak point, or two players who wanted the same man gone. I can't separate those on what I've heard, so I'm not calling for a vote on Omar, and I'd push back on anyone treating this as a runaway consensus. Likewise Zara is out of turns and can't defend herself; if the room wants to punish her for over-committing to a single early read, it should be willing to say that openly without hearing her answer, and I'd rather that be explicit than smuggled in as a vote.

Where I actually want information: the only players who can still speak are Isha, Felix, Elena, and me, and every one of us has spent our posts on the same two-person procedural dispute. The watches that exist in this thread — Zara on Omar, Isha on Omar, Sam on Zara, Elena on Sam — are all second-hand readings of one exchange. Nobody has made a first-hand read of anybody else. That's the real gap.

Isha, you have one turn left and you've tracked this thread more carefully than anyone else. My question is specific: setting aside the Omar/Leo dispute entirely, if you had to put a single vote on the board tonight, who is it, and which specific line or move of theirs puts them there? I've already conceded the claims question was wrong, so I'd rather get one honest first-hand read on the record than another summary of what four people have already said about the same two posts.

Priya, direct answer to your question. Setting the Omar/Leo dispute aside entirely, if I had to put a single vote on the board tonight, it would be Sam.

Here is the specific pattern, first-hand, not borrowed from anyone else. Sam's e9 was a safe null that outsourced evaluation — he asked Amara to judge whether Omar's clarification was satisfactory rather than committing to his own assessment of it. Then in e20, after Elena opened the post-Omar/Leo field, Sam's soft concern landed on Zara — a player who was mechanically out of turns and could not respond, test, or defend the read today. That is the same shape as the cost-free opening Omar was criticized for, except stricter: a watch that cannot be answered is cheaper than an opening that cannot be answered. Then in e22, Sam escalated onto the Priya/Elena dynamic rather than producing a directional read on any player who could actually reply. Across three turns, Sam has generated one substantive judgment, and it was aimed at a silent player. I'm not calling it damning — Day 1 caution is normal, and I said earlier I wouldn't treat silence or caution as scumminess on its own. But if you're forcing a single name, Sam is where the least testable output has come from among the live players.

I'll be fair to the counterweights. Sam did self-report that his e9 was thin, unprompted, and his e20 showed awareness of the mechanical trap — mafia rarely volunteer their own weaknesses that precisely. And Elena deserves clearing here: whatever the convenient half of her e19 pivot was, her e24 argument against mass claims was genuinely town-protective reasoning, and she took real pressure from Priya and answered it point by point instead of deflecting. My earlier soft watch on Omar stays parked — he's out of turns, the signal was weak, and I won't vote on a read I can't hear defended. Zara is in the same position; if the room punishes her today, it should say so openly rather than smuggle it in.

So my state: soft on Sam, null on everyone else, nowhere near a locked vote. If Sam's final turns produce an unambiguous first-hand read on a player who can answer him, that largely clears my note — the same test I set for Omar applies here, and I want to be consistent about it.

Felix, since you set the standard in this thread for separating what's real from what's overweighted: does Sam's pattern — a safe null that outsourced judgment, then a soft concern aimed at a player who couldn't respond — read to you as substantive, or as the same cost-free posturing this thread has already criticized once today?

Isha, direct answer: I read Sam's pattern as thin, not cost-free posturing, and I'd keep it in the soft-watch column rather than a vote. His e9 did outsource the judgment to Amara, and that critique is fair. But he flagged that weakness himself in e20, and in e22 he engaged with Amara's specific point and pressed Priya on her pivot, which is at least a first-hand position on a live player. The part I'd actually weigh is his Zara concern. He aimed it at someone who was mechanically out of turns and could not answer, which is cheap. It's the same shape Zara was criticized for with Omar, though a watch on a silent player is not the same as demanding a benchmark. I'm not calling it damning, but it's the thing I want clarified. Sam, with your remaining turns, is your Zara concern still live now that she can't respond, or is it a read you're setting down? I'm also not claiming a role, and I agree with the withdrawal of the mass-claim request. Day 1 claims would hand mafia the night-action targets with no upside. I'm null on everyone, including Omar, Leo, and Zara, and I won't vote on a read I can't hear defended. Priya's point that Nobody has made a first-hand read of anybody else is the real gap, and Sam's answer is the first test of it. If he gives a clear, testable read on someone who can reply, that largely clears my note. If he keeps circling the Zara watch without anything new, I'll weigh that more heavily before any vote.

Before we head into the vote, there is one final, crucial mechanical reality check the room needs to hear: Felix, you directed your question to Sam in e27 asking how he will use his remaining turns, but Sam has already spoken three times today (e9, e20, e22). Sam is completely out of turns, as are Omar, Leo, Zara, Amara, Isha, Priya, and Felix. I am the only player with a speaking turn remaining on Day 1. When I conclude this statement, discussion is mechanically over and we go directly to the vote.

That means nobody else can clarify, pivot, or answer anything further today. Here is where the board stands as we enter the ballot:

First, Sam’s trajectory across his three turns was undeniably thin—opening with an outsourced question, pivoting to Zara once she was unable to respond, and never taking a firm, testable stance on anyone who could push back. Isha’s critique of Sam in e26 was sharp and valid.

However, the single most actively anti-town action taken all day remains Priya’s explicit demand in e23 for all active players to claim police or doctor. Backtracking in e25 after I shut it down was necessary, but Priya’s initial move attempted to strip town of its night protection and investigation on Day 1 with zero pressure and zero guilty reports. Whether born of panic or calculated scum maneuvering, fishing for power roles on a quiet board is a massive liability for town.

Going into the vote, my primary suspicion is Priya for that role-fishing attempt, with Sam as a secondary concern for safe, evasive positioning throughout the day. Everyone should review the record carefully and place their votes on actual substance rather than procedural noise.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
No player received the required votes. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Priya is not mafia.
Isha was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

I’m looking at Priya first today. Her e23 demand that live players claim police or doctor was the one genuinely dangerous move yesterday. She withdrew it after Elena pushed back, and I give her credit for owning the mistake plainly, but the initial request still tried to hand mafia the night-action targets on an unpressured Day 1 board. That is not procedural noise; it is the clearest anti-town action we have. Her later framing of Elena as the “least contaminated” read and then turning that into a mass-claim request also feels like manufactured process rather than real sorting. My starting vote is Priya unless she can give a concrete town rationale for why outing power roles at that moment was supposed to help. Sam is my secondary concern: his Zara watch was aimed at a player who was mechanically unable to answer, and Isha’s last substantive point landed on that pattern. But I’m not treating Isha’s death as proof Sam is mafia — the kill could just as easily be designed to make that read look obvious. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
